word:lxx:L700058.explanation: Abigaian is a proper name, given in the Greek Old Testament as “Abigaian” or “Aviyean.” It identifies a named person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This LXX word occurs twice, once in 1 Samuel 25:40 and once in 2 Samuel 17:25. Without the surrounding verse text, no further contextual detail about the person can be stated safely.

word:lxx:L700061.explanation: Abidan is a proper name referring to a person. It is rendered as “Abidan” and is also associated with the form “Avithan.” In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs five times, all in the book of Numbers. The name appears in lists and records concerning Israel’s tribes and leaders, but the name itself identifies the person rather than describing a quality, action, or role. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and account.

word:lxx:L700164.explanation: The word means a “hook,” a shaped implement used to catch, hold, or draw something. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing once each in 2 Kings, Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Habakkuk. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and image, but its ordinary lexical meaning remains a hook.

word:lxx:L700263.explanation: This LXX adjective describes someone or something that remains unswerving and undeterred rather than being turned aside. It expresses steadfast direction, purpose, or resolve in the face of opposition or pressure. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament translation, in 3 Maccabees 3:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is firm persistence without deviation.

word:lxx:L700339.explanation: Aziph, also rendered Azif, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person or place by name rather than expressing an action, quality, or idea. This name occurs twice in the LXX, both times in Joshua, at Joshua 11:1 and Joshua 12:20. Without the surrounding verse text, the name’s specific referent cannot be described further here; its basic meaning is the proper designation Aziph or Azif.

word:lxx:L700366.explanation: Faithlessness describes a lack of faithfulness—failure to remain loyal, trustworthy, or committed. As a noun or describing word, it identifies this condition rather than a specific action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Jeremiah and twice in Maccabees. The central meaning remains “faithlessness”; the surrounding passage determines whether the word highlights an unfaithful attitude, conduct, or relationship. It is a concise term for departing from dependable fidelity.

word:lxx:L700432.explanation: This word is a proper name meaning “Ailameitēs” or “Elamitis.” It identifies the named subject rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 11:11. The available lexical information preserves the name but does not provide the verse’s surrounding wording, so its precise role in that sentence must be determined from the passage itself. Its basic function remains identification.

word:lxx:L700634.explanation: This word means salt, the common substance named by the noun. It names salt rather than describing an action or quality. In this Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus, it occurs six times, each represented by the English rendering “salt.” Its appearances range from Leviticus through Sirach, so the word is used across several books while retaining the same basic meaning. The precise significance of salt in any particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding text.

word:lxx:L700803.explanation: This verb means being unconcerned or negligent—failing to give something the attention, care, or seriousness it requires. It describes an attitude or action of disregarding responsibility rather than actively opposing something. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs four times, appearing in both Jeremiah and later wisdom and historical writings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what person or duty is being neglected.

word:lxx:L700894.explanation: Amōkē is a proper name, represented in English as Amoke. It functions as a personal or place-name designation rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs only once, at Joshua 18:26. The name itself identifies the named subject in that passage, while the surrounding verse determines whether it refers to a person, location, or another named entity. No broader lexical meaning is given for Amōkē beyond its use as a proper name.

word:lxx:L700919.explanation: This word is a proper name referring to a named entity called “Anabōth,” also rendered “Anavoth.” It is not a general term describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 11:21. The lexical information identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular role in that passage there.

word:lxx:L700946.explanation: “Rekindle” means to kindle something again, restoring a fire or its active strength after it has faded. It is a verb, so it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In this Greek biblical corpus, it occurs twice, once in Genesis and once in 1 Maccabees. The central idea is renewal: something that had diminished is made burning or active again. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse.

word:lxx:L701105.explanation: Androgynaios means effeminate, or like an effeminate man.

word:lxx:L701170.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something that has not been defeated or cannot be overcome. It can therefore emphasize steadfastness, resistance, or victory over opposition, depending on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs six times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 2, 3, and 4 Maccabees. Its central idea remains the same: being unconquered in fact or unconquerable in strength. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on an achieved victory or an enduring quality.

word:lxx:L701242.explanation: “Opposite” means directly facing or positioned across from something. As an adverb, this word describes how or where an action or position relates to another: it points to being opposite rather than merely nearby or different. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:16. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, which is not included here.

policy.priorReviewerNotes: The candidate treats the supplied proper-name entry as a common lexical item and asserts a meaning not established by LEX_DEF, which contains only the form. The Scripture renderings support related English wording but do not cure the lexical-category mismatch.

word:lxx:L701343.explanation: This verb means to “have the effrontery to do” something—to act with bold disregard for what would normally restrain a person. It describes the act of daring to proceed despite shame, embarrassment, or the impropriety of the action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Jeremiah 3:3. Its exact force in that verse is understood more fully from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the audacity to do what one should hesitate to do.

word:lxx:L701444.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “breastband” or “girdle,” referring to a band or fastening worn around the body. It names a physical clothing item rather than an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Song of Songs 1:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a breastband or girdle.

word:lxx:L701501.explanation: This verb means “hinder”: to hold someone or something back so that movement or action is obstructed. It describes an active restraint rather than merely being delayed or unable to proceed. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, including several passages in 1 Samuel and 1 Kings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding sentence says is being hindered.

word:lxx:L701538.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to drive someone from house and home—to banish or force that person away. It describes an action of removing someone from a place or community, rather than merely asking the person to leave. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but its central idea remains expulsion from one’s home or established place.

word:lxx:L701620.explanation: This adjective describes something cut off, abrupt, or sharply ended rather than gradual. It can characterize an action, judgment, movement, or change that happens suddenly or decisively, depending on the sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in the book of Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what it modifies and the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L701655.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “light.” As a verb, it expresses an action involving light rather than naming a person, object, or quality. Its exact force in a verse depends on what is being acted upon and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of lighting. It occurs 22 times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, including one occurrence in Wisdom.

word:lxx:L701682.explanation: Aram is a proper name, rendered “Aram.” In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 11 times in 11 verses, from Genesis through Isaiah, including genealogical passages and other Old Testament references. Its exact referent in any particular verse must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text, but the word itself functions as the name Aram.

word:lxx:L701736.explanation: This noun means a “joint”: a connecting part of the body where separate bones or parts meet. It identifies the joint itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in 4 Maccabees. The basic meaning remains bodily and concrete; the surrounding verse determines what is said about that joint.

word:lxx:L701769.explanation: This word is a proper name: “Armathaim,” also given as “Armathem.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 12 times, all in 1 Samuel, so its meaning is chiefly the name itself rather than a broader descriptive idea. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what the named entity is doing or how it relates to the passage.

word:lxx:L702052.explanation: Aschanazaios is a proper name, appearing as “Aschanazaios” or “Askhanazeos.” It identifies a particular person or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Jeremiah 28:27. Because it is a name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function; the surrounding verse is needed to explain whom it identifies there.

word:lxx:L702085.explanation: This verb means “stare”: to look steadily and intently at someone or something. It describes a sustained gaze rather than a brief glance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 2:26. The word identifies the act of fixing one’s eyes on an object or person, while the surrounding passage determines the specific reason, emotion, or significance of that gaze.

word:lxx:L702148.explanation: Auranos, also rendered Avranos, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 4:40. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide surrounding verse text, so it does not establish further details about the person or referent identified there.

word:lxx:L702306.explanation: This word means “thistle,” a prickly plant. It is a noun used to name this kind of vegetation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Chronicles 25:18. The word therefore identifies a physical plant rather than an action, quality, or person. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its comparison or description there.

word:lxx:L702359.explanation: Bagoi, also rendered Vayi, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezra and Nehemiah, including lists of returned families and community members. Without the surrounding verse text, the individual’s specific identity and role cannot be stated securely from the name alone.

word:lxx:L702430.explanation: Baithsamys, also rendered Vethsamis, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named place or location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs 20 times across 18 Old Testament verses, beginning in Joshua and continuing through 2 Chronicles. It appears several times in Joshua and 1 Samuel, showing that it is used as a recurring geographical name within Israel’s biblical history.

word:lxx:L702445.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “walk” or “step,” describing movement from one place to another. It can refer to the act of walking generally or to taking a step. The word appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Deuteronomy, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a person, or possibly something described as moving, advances by walking or stepping. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on ordinary movement or on the manner and direction of that movement.

word:lxx:L702517.explanation: This verb means “dip”: to place or lower something into a substance. It describes an action performed on an object, rather than a person, place, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times across 15 verses, showing repeated use for this straightforward physical action. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being dipped and what substance is involved.

word:lxx:L702588.explanation: This noun refers to slander or envy—harmful speech about another person or resentful ill will toward what another has or is. It can name either the damaging expression or the inward attitude behind it, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in deuterocanonical books. Its basic sense therefore points to a destructive attitude or action that injures another through jealous feeling or harmful speech.

word:lxx:L702702.explanation: Bērsabee is a name used for a place and for a woman.

word:lxx:L702867.explanation: This word means “crystal,” referring to a clear, glasslike substance. It is a noun, naming a material rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 28:18. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a transparent, crystal-like substance. The word belongs specifically to the Greek LXX vocabulary and should not be merged with a Greek New Testament word merely because an English translation may use a similar term.

word:lxx:L702913.explanation: Gaithbōr; Yethvor is a proper name, functioning as a specific name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 19:22. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not specify whether it refers to a person, place, or other named entity. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding passage and the biblical text at that location.

word:lxx:L702984.explanation: This verb means to pride oneself or exalt oneself—to lift oneself up with a sense of superiority or self-importance. It describes an action or attitude rather than simply possessing a good quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in deuterocanonical writings. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains self-exaltation or taking pride in oneself.

word:lxx:L703015.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “neighbour” or “border on”: it describes being next to another person, place, or area, or sharing a boundary with it. As a verb, it expresses adjacency rather than movement toward something. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 9:25. The precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic idea is closeness or a common border.

word:lxx:L703060.explanation: Gerara is a proper name for a place, also rendered “Yerara.” It identifies a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 11 times, appearing mainly in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. The name is found in passages such as Genesis 10:19, Genesis 20:1–2, and Genesis 26:1, 6, and 8. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative.

word:lxx:L703204.explanation: This verb means “naked,” describing a person who is without clothing. It functions as an action word for being in that condition rather than naming a person, object, or place. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Genesis 9:21. The word’s basic meaning is limited and concrete; the surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular situation in which it appears.

word:lxx:L703293.explanation: Darkōn, also rendered Tharkon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 2:56, identifying a person or family in that passage. The name itself does not provide a further lexical description, so its precise significance depends on the surrounding Ezra context. This Greek LXX name should be kept distinct from similarly rendered names or words in other biblical language traditions.

word:lxx:L703341.explanation: This adverb means “tenfold,” describing something multiplied or increased by ten. It expresses a ten-times comparison or amount rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 1:20. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains a tenfold measure or degree.

word:lxx:L703378.explanation: This verb means “lord of; master of,” describing the act of ruling over or exercising mastery. It presents someone as holding authority over another person or thing, rather than merely possessing it. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:28. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense is authority expressed through mastery or rule. word:lxx:L703411.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “public,” describing something connected with what is open or common rather than private. It is used 208 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, with most occurrences in Numbers and Joshua. The word’s basic sense remains broad: it identifies something belonging to public life or shared openly. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject.

word:lxx:L703428.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “devilish” or “devil,” referring to an evil adversary or accuser. It can identify a being presented as opposing or accusing others, while “devilish” describes the character associated with such opposition. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, with its greatest concentration in Job. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains an adversarial, evil figure or character.

word:lxx:L703572.explanation: This LXX Greek verb means to “make thoroughly manifest”—to bring something fully into the open or make it clearly known. As a verb, it describes the act of explaining, revealing, or making a matter unmistakable rather than merely mentioning it. It occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books represented here, including Deuteronomy, Daniel, and 1–2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being made clear in that passage.

word:lxx:L703727.explanation: This verb means to become very angry or to be very angry at someone or something. It describes intense anger rather than mild irritation. In the Greek LXX material, it appears twice, both times in 3 Maccabees, at 3 Maccabees 3:1 and 4:13. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify exactly what provoked the anger in each occurrence, but the word itself clearly expresses strong displeasure or fury.

word:lxx:L703781.explanation: This word means “beam,” referring to a substantial piece of wood used in construction or as part of a building. It is a noun describing structural timber, such as the wooden supports of a house or other structure. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all within six verses, and its ordinary sense remains concrete and practical rather than abstract. The surrounding verse determines the particular building or object in view.

word:lxx:L703824.explanation: This noun means “handful” or “hand,” referring to an amount that can be held in the hand or to the hand itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used six times, including descriptions of offerings, a small quantity of flour, and a hand associated with divine action. Its basic sense remains concrete: a hand, or what a hand can contain. The surrounding passage determines whether it describes the body part or a measured amount.

word:lxx:L703910.explanation: This word means “5” and functions as an indeclinable number, identifying the quantity five. It is a numerical marker rather than a word describing a person, action, or spiritual quality. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, in Psalm 118:33. Its basic meaning is therefore precise and limited: it tells the reader that five items, persons, or units are being counted, while the surrounding verse determines what is being numbered.

word:lxx:L704018.explanation: This word means “I,” referring to the speaker or person presenting himself or herself in a sentence. It is a pronoun, so it identifies the person who speaks, acts, experiences something, or makes a statement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 1,352 times, showing that it is a common way for a speaker to refer directly to himself or herself. Its exact emphasis in any passage depends on the surrounding words and context.

word:lxx:L704021.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “level,” describing the action of making something level or bringing it down to a level surface. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX, appearing across Psalms, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, and Nahum. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the leveling or flattening of something.

word:lxx:L704087.explanation: This adverb means “in all likelihood” or “suitably,” expressing that something is reasonably expected or appropriately done. It can describe a conclusion that makes good sense or an action that fits the circumstances. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 9:2. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is to qualify an action, judgment, or statement as fitting or probable.

word:lxx:L704296.explanation: Ekprepes means distinguished above others or preeminent.

word:lxx:L704362.explanation: This noun means “carrying out,” referring to the act or process of taking something out or bringing it forth. It names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within two verses in 2 Chronicles. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but its central sense remains the carrying out of something.

word:lxx:L704414.explanation: This noun means “conviction”: a firm inner persuasion that something is true or demands acknowledgment. It names the settled recognition produced when a matter is brought clearly before the mind, rather than an outward action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job, showing a focused use rather than a broadly repeated term. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument.

word:lxx:L704483.explanation: This proper name refers to Elisha, the prophet known by this name in the Greek Old Testament. It is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears 98 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scripture represented here, with nearly all occurrences in 1–2 Kings and one in Sirach. Because it identifies a person, its meaning is primarily the person’s name; the surrounding passage is needed to understand what is being said about Elisha in any particular verse.

word:lxx:L704609.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “get by barter”: to obtain or conduct a transaction through exchange rather than ordinary purchase. It describes the act of trading goods or value with another person. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Amos 8:5, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic idea is gaining something through bargaining or exchange.

word:lxx:L704700.explanation: Endysis means dressing in, or putting on apparel.

word:lxx:L705017.explanation: This verb means “renew” or “revive”: to make something fresh, active, or strong again. It describes restoration rather than merely beginning something for the first time. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, this word occurs once, at Job 10:17. That single occurrence shows that its basic sense is focused and specific, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what is being renewed or revived there.

word:lxx:L705202.explanation: This adjective describes something that is somewhat long or oblong in shape. It points to an elongated form rather than a perfectly round or evenly proportioned one. As an adjective, it modifies a person, object, or other noun by describing its outward shape or proportions. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Baruch 3:24; the reference identifies where the word appears, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what it describes there.

word:lxx:L705448.explanation: This adjective describes something enclosed, protected, or made strong against attack: “fenced; fortified.” It points to the defensive character of a place or structure, emphasizing security and resistance rather than ordinary openness. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is clear: a place secured by defenses.

word:lxx:L705471.explanation: Eseban, also Esevan, is a personal name.

word:lxx:L705552.explanation: This noun means “abundance of men” or “store of goodly men”—a substantial group of men regarded as goodly. It refers to a gathered supply or strength of people rather than to one individual. In the Greek text of 2 Maccabees, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees 8:7 and 15:17. The precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word’s central idea is a plentiful body of men, especially viewed as a useful or worthy resource.

word:lxx:L705585.explanation: This noun refers to fine weather or a pleasant, favorable day. It describes good conditions in the day rather than a person, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. The word can therefore point to the goodness or pleasantness of the day’s conditions, with the surrounding sentence determining its precise use. Its central idea remains favorable weather or a fine day.

word:lxx:L705606.explanation: Euilat, also rendered Eilat, is a proper name used for a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament. The name itself does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual idea; it identifies someone or somewhere named Euilat. It occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis, 1 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. The surrounding verse is needed to determine whether each occurrence refers to a person or a location.

word:lxx:L705659.explanation: Eupatora is a proper name used to identify a person, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is the name “Eupatora.” In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 2 Maccabees: 2 Maccabees 2:20; 10:10; 10:13; and 13:1. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain which person is being named in each occurrence.

word:lxx:L705754.explanation: This adjective means “easy to reach; accessible.” It describes something that can be approached or attained without being out of reach. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 15:38. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context, but its ordinary sense is clear: something available, approachable, or within reach.

word:lxx:L706074.explanation: This noun refers to “courses of stones,” meaning arranged rows or layers of stone. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, at Song of Songs 4:4. The word therefore names a physical stone arrangement rather than an action, quality, or person. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here, but its basic meaning remains a set of stones placed in successive courses.

word:lxx:L706225.explanation: Thessamys is a proper name, also rendered Thessamis. It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:38. Because the available wording does not identify whether the name refers to a person, place, or another named entity, its safest meaning is simply the proper designation Thessamys. Its specific significance must be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

word:lxx:L706250.explanation: This adjective describes something that has been captured or taken by wild animals. It identifies the condition of an animal or other living thing after such an encounter, rather than naming the act of capture itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, showing a specific meaning used in passages dealing with animals, loss, and what has been found or handled. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:lxx:L706467.explanation: Iachirani, also rendered Iakhirani, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Numbers 26:42. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not specify beyond that what person, family, or group it identifies in the verse.

word:lxx:L706513.explanation: Iebatha, also rendered Ievatha, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person, place, or other entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition, though the available information does not specify which kind of entity it names. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 21:25. Its exact referent is determined by the surrounding passage, not by the name itself.

word:lxx:L706584.explanation: Iemēr, also rendered Iemir, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:61. The available lexical information identifies the name itself but does not provide its meaning as a common noun or explain the person’s identity. Its specific significance in that passage therefore comes from the surrounding list and context, not from the name alone.

word:lxx:L706751.explanation: This is a proper name, given as “Indos” or “Inthos.” It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 6:37. The available lexical information does not specify from the name alone whether the named entity is a person or place, so its precise referent must come from the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L706768.explanation: This word is a proper name rendered “Iouda” or “Iutha.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, it occurs 673 times, so it is a recurring name across the text. word:lxx:L713106.explanation: Hypatos means highest, describing superior rank or authority.

word:lxx:L713159.explanation: This verb means “melt exceedingly,” describing something undergoing an intense or complete melting. As a verb, it expresses an action or process rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:12. The word’s exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the idea of melting to an extreme degree.

word:lxx:L713252.explanation: This noun means “at the breast,” describing a nursing infant or one still being fed at the breast. It presents the person as dependent on a mother for nourishment rather than able to feed independently. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Hosea 14:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to the condition of being at the breast.

word:lxx:L713285.explanation: Hypsēlos means high. It can also mean lofty, describing something elevated above others.

word:lxx:L713348.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “play a role” or “act in pretence.” It describes behaving as though one is someone or something else, presenting an appearance rather than acting plainly and sincerely. As a verb, it expresses this kind of performed behavior. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 4:30; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise force there.

word:lxx:L713371.explanation: Pharnach, also known as Farnakh, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Numbers 34:25. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes the person’s designation but does not provide further information about his identity, role, character, or significance. Its meaning is therefore best stated simply as the personal name Pharnach or Farnakh.

word:lxx:L713502.explanation: This adjective describes someone who loves honor or is covetous of honor. It points to a strong desire for esteem or recognition, rather than simply identifying a person who receives honor. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Wisdom and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains a person or attitude marked by a desire for honor.

word:lxx:L713630.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “mix”: to combine things so that they are blended together. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 20:12; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains the act of mixing or blending, whether referring to materials or things brought together.

word:lxx:L713645.explanation: Phōteinos means luminous, bright with light.

word:lxx:L713692.explanation: Chalkeuō means to make of copper.

word:lxx:L713829.explanation: Chermel, also rendered Khermel, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available material does not specify which in each occurrence. The name appears six times across four verses, in Joshua and Isaiah. Its exact reference depends on the surrounding verse, yet its basic function remains that of a name: it identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing a general idea.

word:lxx:L713876.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to an ornament worn for decoration, especially a bracelet. It names a personal adornment rather than an action or quality. In its five occurrences across the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical text, it is used for jewelry or decorative objects associated with people. The word may describe one bracelet or ornaments generally, but its central meaning remains a visible item worn to adorn the body.

word:lxx:L713968.explanation: This word is a noun that names a person, place, thing, or idea. Its basic sense is “short time”. It refers to a brief span of time rather than an extended period. As a noun, it can name this limited duration when the surrounding sentence focuses on how long something lasts or how soon it may change. In the Greek text represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:1. That single occurrence confirms its limited use in this corpus, while the definition keeps the central idea clear: a short period of time.

word:lxx:L714077.explanation: Psōmizō means to provide food or feed someone.

word:lxx:L714132.explanation: Hōraios means attractive, describing something beautiful to the eye; it can describe the visible appearance of a tree.
